message.content:
The total number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of **10⁴³**.  

This figure comes from an estimate known as the *Shannon number*, named after Claude Shannon. It is derived by multiplying the average branching factor (≈30) raised to the average length of a game (≈80 moves), and then adjusting for constraints such as repetition rules and illegal positions. The result is roughly:

\[
\text{Number of positions} \approx 10^{43}\text{–}10^{44}
\]

So while there are about \(10^{120}\) possible games (sequences of moves), the sheer variety of unique board configurations you could encounter during play is about \(10^{43}\).
